evaluation.positioning_hook: A small-town podcaster and a school custodian uncover a buried trafficking network running through a church, a police department, and a high school before the town’s power structure buries them first.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The missing-girl engine, institutional corruption, and podcast-investigation frame give this a clear thriller audience with strong streaming appeal. It’s not four-quadrant, but the premise is easy to sell and the stakes are immediate.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands fast: a local podcast starts with one runaway girl and opens into a hidden network tied to the school and church. The act-one reveal of altered records and the act-two tunnel system make the premise easy to explain in two sentences.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Ralph and Savannah are functional and playable, with a nice contrast between his quiet custodial access and her on-air drive. They’re more effective as competent investigators than as deeply surprising characters, and the supporting cast is mostly defined by function.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The podcast-plus-small-town-corruption lane is familiar, but the custodial protagonist and church/school tunnel infrastructure give it a more specific local texture. The execution is solidly commercial rather than especially daring.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps escalating from one missing girl to multiple victims, then to a hidden operation and a named power figure. The forward motion is clear, though several beats are delivered as investigation reveals rather than scene-level reversals.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The buried-system reveal is satisfying and the school/church/police triangle gives the story a clean moral map. It feels fresh in details, but the underlying shape is a recognizable conspiracy thriller.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The town has usable story texture: high school football culture, church authority, police hierarchy, and a local podcast ecosystem all feed the plot. The tunnel network and rotating “Director” position add a specific institutional mythology.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is consistent and grounded, with a procedural-thriller seriousness and a local-color opening. It doesn’t yet have a highly singular tonal signature beyond competent, gritty suspense.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The “Director” concept, the older power structure, and the final tag implying the system continues all suggest a larger hidden history. There’s enough here to imply a broader conspiracy world without overexplaining it.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Ralph and Savannah have the clearest recurring dynamic, and Daniels/Tingling add pressure, but the ensemble mostly serves the case. There’s usable friction, though not a lot of relationship-based story generation beyond the investigation itself.

lead_characters.name: Ralph Cipplone
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s, working-class local custodian/janitor, white, small-town Pennsylvania.
lead_characters.hook: Ralph is the quiet, observant guy who knows the building better than anyone and notices what everyone else walks past. He reads as steady and unshowy, but the script gives him a buried intensity: he’s the one who can move through the school, church, and tunnel spaces without looking like he belongs to the conspiracy, which makes him dangerous to it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Bryan Cranston in Breaking Bad or Michael Keaton in Spotlight: a contained, watchful lead whose authority comes from restraint, then flips into moral force. It gives an actor the chance to play stillness, intelligence, and late-breaking heroism in the same role.

lead_characters.name: Savannah McMullen
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, local podcaster/journalist, white, professionally ambitious, small-town Pennsylvania.
lead_characters.hook: Savannah is the public voice of the investigation: quick, skeptical, and willing to put herself on the line once the story turns real. She has the best forward momentum in the script and functions as the pressure valve between the audience and the conspiracy, with enough confidence to push against authority without losing warmth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the sharp, propulsive newsroom energy of Rachel McAdams in Spotlight or Jodie Comer in The Last Duel: smart, relentless, and emotionally present under pressure. It offers a strong on-camera voice role with urgency, credibility, and a clear moral center.

lead_characters.name: Chief Daniels
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 50s-60s, police chief, white, local power broker with compromised authority.
lead_characters.hook: Daniels is the institutional hinge: he starts as an obstacle, then becomes a partial truth-teller, then a man trying to control the collapse of the system he helped maintain. He’s written with enough ambiguity to keep him useful as both suspect and ally.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor material in the lane of Jeffrey Wright in The Batman or Shea Whigham in any corruption thriller: a role built on controlled menace, fatigue, and strategic ambiguity. It gives an actor the chance to play a man whose face changes meaning as the story unfolds.

lead_characters.name: Rick Tingling
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 70s, elderly local power figure, white, polished and controlled.
lead_characters.hook: Tingling is the face of the machine: calm, refined, and terrifying because he treats the operation like administration rather than crime. The script makes him feel like a legacy villain, someone who has survived by becoming the system itself.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-career villain role that gives an actor the prestige menace of John Lithgow in Dexter or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor: elegant, controlled, and quietly monstrous. It’s a scene-stealing part with authority and a memorable final confrontation.

lead_characters.name: Kayla Morris
lead_characters.demographics: Female, teen, missing girl / survivor, likely white, vulnerable but alert.
lead_characters.hook: Kayla is the emotional proof that the conspiracy is real, not just procedural noise. She’s not just a victim; the script gives her the crucial moment of recognition and fear that turns the investigation from theory into rescue.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can make a young actor in the vein of Kaitlyn Dever in Short Term 12 or Cailee Spaeny in Priscilla stand out fast: brief but emotionally loaded, with a single scene that has to land hard. It’s a survival-role showcase with real audience sympathy.

casting_characteristics: One lead role built around restrained authority and physical credibility
Older antagonist role for a late-70s actor
Teen survivor role with emotional vulnerability
Ensemble of law-enforcement and local authority types

notable_requirements: High school football field and interior school spaces
Church sanctuary, office, basement, and tunnel access
Police department, archive room, interrogation room, hospital, podcast studio
Underground tunnel set or practical subterranean location

technical.vfx_details: No apparent VFX requirement beyond basic compositing or cleanup.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical fight beats, car impact, flashlight-driven suspense, police raid coverage.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: contained theatrical-or-streaming thriller with strong streamer upside.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly contained, but the school, church, police, hospital, podcast studio, and tunnel spaces create a location count that can creep if not consolidated.

casting.note: Ralph needs a very specific blend of quiet authority and physical credibility, while Tingling needs an older actor who can play polished menace without turning theatrical.

development.note: The conspiracy reveal is clear, but the script leans on investigation beats and exposition-heavy reveals more than character-driven reversals in the second half.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like grounded conspiracy thrillers with local texture, moral stakes, and a procedural investigation spine.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, slight male skew but viable for women; middle-income to upper-middle-income viewers who watch prestige crime and true-crime-adjacent thrillers.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary, dialogue-forward, and location-based, with modest stunt work and no VFX load; the tunnel and night coverage are the main scope drivers.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the grounded, adult-skewing thriller lane where local institutions hide a larger rot. The podcast frame gives it a contemporary hook, while the school/church/police triangle keeps it squarely in prestige-crime territory.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the conspiracy resolves as a single case, and no secondary character is developed enough to anchor a clean spinoff.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The school-church-police triangle is cleanly ownable.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a simple moral map buyers can market fast: trusted institutions are the threat, not the rescue. It’s the kind of premise that attracts streamer thriller buyers and prestige-crime audiences looking for a local conspiracy with a clear villain system.
strengths.evidence: The act-one clue trail moves from the school hallway to St. Andrew’s Church to the police archive room, with altered records and tunnel access tying them together.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ralph is a strong low-key lead engine.
strengths.what_it_means: A quiet custodian who can move through the story’s physical spaces gives the film a distinctive access point and a playable star role. That kind of restrained, working-class lead is attractive to character actors and buyers looking for a grounded anchor rather than a procedural template.
strengths.evidence: Ralph is introduced mopping the school after the game, then becomes the one who spots the name, enters the basement, and later goes alone into the church.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The podcast frame modernizes the investigation.
strengths.what_it_means: The Off The Record setup gives the movie a contemporary entry point without forcing it into a tech-thriller lane. It helps the script feel current to streamers and gives marketing a clean public-facing hook.
strengths.evidence: Savannah and Ralph use the podcast to receive the first tip, discuss whether to go public, and close the film with a broadcasted truth statement.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tunnel reveal expands the world without blowing the budget.
strengths.what_it_means: A hidden infrastructure under familiar locations creates scale and conspiracy energy while staying producible as a practical set or limited build. That’s a useful sweet spot for buyers who want scope without tentpole spend.
strengths.evidence: The church floor opens to a tunnel system connecting the school and church, with organized movement, files, and a holding room beneath the town.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The older villain gives the climax a prestige face.
strengths.what_it_means: Rick Tingling as the refined, elderly architect of the system creates a memorable final antagonist role that can attract a serious character actor. Buyers often respond to a thriller that can promise one scene-stealing elder villain rather than a faceless conspiracy.
strengths.evidence: Tingling is introduced as the Director, speaks in controlled aphorisms, and gets the final confrontation in the tunnel chamber.

whats_special.headline: This is a clean, marketable prestige-thriller package: a grounded small-town conspiracy with a modern podcast frame, a distinctive working-class lead, and a contained production footprint. The script’s best commercial asset is that it feels bigger than its budget without needing VFX or franchise machinery.

items.area: Savannah reads more functional than indispensable.
items.detail: She drives the investigation, but the script gives Ralph the more distinctive access point and the more unusual physical role. That makes the lead/partner balance feel slightly asymmetrical in a way buyers will notice when they think about who the movie is really built around.

items.area: The second half leans on explanation.
items.detail: Once the task force board, the initials K.D., and the “Director” reveal arrive, the script spends a lot of time naming the system rather than dramatizing new turns. That’s a manageable development note, but it does flatten some of the momentum after the act-two midpoint.

items.area: The conspiracy is broader than the character work.
items.detail: The school, church, police, and tunnel network are all compelling, but most supporting players function as conduits for information rather than as fully differentiated pressure points. That keeps the ensemble efficient, but it limits relationship density beyond the central duo.

The final tunnel confrontation, gunfire, and public cuffing of the villain land cleanly, but the shape is recognizable within the conspiracy-thriller lane. Buyers will likely respond to the execution more than to any surprise in the ending architecture.

issues.headline: The main friction is not premise clarity; it’s that the script’s strongest access point belongs to Ralph, while Savannah carries much of the procedural load. The second half also shifts toward explanation-heavy conspiracy mechanics, which makes the final stretch feel more competent than revelatory.
